Shout at a cliff and your voice comes back a moment later: an **echo**. A **delay** effect records the
sound and plays it back a set time later, mixed in with the original. Feed some of that copy back into
the delay and it repeats again, and again, each time quieter. It's the simplest effect there is, and
the building block of [chorus and flanger](sound-chorus.qmd) and of most of [reverb](sound-reverb.qmd).

**How to use the page.** The source starts as **single hits**, so each echo is easy to hear. The strip
under the controls shows one hit and every echo that follows it, as tall as it is loud.

## The echo

<div class="sk" data-w="delay" data-source="hits"></div>

- **Delay time**: how long until the copy comes back. Under about 30 ms you don't hear an echo at all,
  just a thicker sound (that's where chorus and flanger live). From about 60 to 150 ms you hear a
  **slapback**. Longer, and you hear separate repeats.
- **Feedback**: how much of each echo is sent round again. 0% is a single echo; 50% means each repeat is
  half as loud as the last. Push it past 100% and every repeat is *louder*: the echoes pile up into a
  roar (this delay squashes them so they can't blow up; real tape echoes do the same).
- **Tone of the repeats**: a low-pass inside the loop, so every trip round loses more top end. The
  echoes get darker as they fade, which is what tape and old analog delays did and why they sit
  so well behind the music.
- **Wow and flutter**: tape never runs at quite a steady speed. A slow wobble (wow) and a fast one
  (flutter) bend the pitch of the repeats.
- **Ping-pong**: two delays feeding each other, one on the left and one on the right, so the echoes
  bounce between your ears. Headphones on.

## The presets

| Preset | Where you've heard it |
|---|---|
| **Slapback** | 1950s rock 'n' roll: Elvis's voice and Scotty Moore's guitar at Sun Records, one quick echo from a second tape machine |
| **Echo** | a voice in a big space, a few repeats |
| **Dotted eighth** | the Edge (U2): the echo lands between the notes, so a plain run of eighth notes becomes a sixteenth-note pattern. Try it on the **Synth riff** |
| **Ping-pong** | a stereo bounce, timed to the beat |
| **Tape echo** | a Roland Space Echo or an Echoplex: dark, wobbly repeats |
| **Dub** | King Tubby and Lee "Scratch" Perry: long, dark repeats that hang on after the band drops out |
| **Runaway** | feedback over 100%. While it plays, drag the **Delay time**: the repeats slide in pitch, the way a tape echo does when you turn its speed knob |

**Timing to the beat.** At a tempo of *B* beats per minute, one beat lasts 60000 ÷ *B* milliseconds.
The riff here is at 112 bpm, so a quarter note is 536 ms, an eighth note 268 ms, and a dotted eighth
(three sixteenths) 402 ms. Most delays have a tap button or tempo sync to do this for you.

## Glitch: stutter and beat repeat

Electronic producers break the music on purpose. One of the commonest tricks is the **stutter** (or
**beat repeat**): grab a tiny slice of the music and loop it, *rat-a-tat-tat*, for a beat or two.

It's a delay used in a strange way. The delay time is set to the length of one slice. When a glitch
fires, the input is cut and the feedback goes to exactly 100%, so the last slice goes round and
round, never fading. When the glitch ends, the music comes back.

<div class="sk" data-w="glitch" data-source="drums"></div>

- **Slice**: how long the looped bit is. Short slices (1/32, 1/64) loop so fast they buzz with a pitch
  of their own.
- **Chance**: how likely a glitch is on each half beat. Press **Glitch now** to fire one yourself.
- **Pitch drift**: the delay time shrinks (or grows) while the slice loops, so the repeats get faster
  and rise (a **riser**) or slow down and fall (a **tape stop**).
- **Crush the repeats** and **backwards slices** add the other two classic glitch sounds: a
  [bit crusher](sound-distortion.qmd) and a slice played in reverse.

Glitch effects are everywhere in electronic dance music, in Aphex Twin and Squarepusher, in trap
hi-hat rolls, and in vocal chops in pop. Plug-ins like Ableton's Beat Repeat and iZotope's Stutter Edit
are built on this idea. Used for a beat at the end of a phrase, it's a fill; used everywhere, it's
annoying. Try your **Microphone** and say a sentence while it plays.
